deed: אהוד שפירא בנה ממולקולות DNA את המחשב הקטן בעולם שמאבחן סרטן
title: Ehud Shapiro and his team at the Weizmann Institute built a tiny computer made of DNA that identified signs of cancer in a test tube

trailer.text: He and researchers at Israel's Weizmann Institute built the world's smallest biomolecular computer, whose input, output and software are made of DNA molecules.

In 2004 they reported in Nature on a version that was programmed to identify, in a test tube, RNA molecules that indicate prostate cancer. After a correct diagnosis, it released short DNA strands designed to kill cancer cells.
The team also identified, in a test tube, signs of one form of lung cancer.
The researchers hope one day to create a doctor in a cell that will operate inside a living body, identify disease and treat it before symptoms appear.

glance.label: First version
glance.value: 2001, simple calculations in a test tube

glance.label: Size
glance.value: A trillion computers in a drop of water

stations.title: Before: a DNA computer is still an idea

paragraphs.text: According to Chemistry World, about a decade before 2004 the scientist Leonard Adleman demonstrated the first DNA-based computation, and surprised the world.
It was only a proof of principle. The task was simple, but required an enormous amount of laboratory work.
Shapiro was a novice in biology when he realized a first design for a molecular computer, as a LEGO-like mechanical device. The design was patented upon his return to the Weizmann Institute in 1998.
In 2001 Shapiro and his colleagues introduced the original version of the biomolecular computer, which performed simple mathematical calculations in a test tube.
In the biological computers from his laboratory, the input, output and software are made of DNA, and enzymes serve as the hardware.
Shapiro made international headlines for a programmable molecular computing machine, built of enzymes and DNA molecules.

stations.title: 2003: a computer whose input is also its fuel

paragraphs.text: In 2003 an improved system was reported.
In this version, the single DNA molecule that provides the input data also provides all the necessary fuel.
The device breaks two bonds in the input molecule and releases the energy stored in them as heat.
According to Guinness, a microlitre of salt solution containing 3 trillion DNA devices performs 66 billion operations per second.
According to the press release, a spoonful of computer soup can contain 15,000 trillion such computers. Together they perform 330 trillion operations per second, with 99.9% accuracy per step.
According to Guinness, the results were announced on 24 February 2003 in the journal PNAS.

The study was carried out by Yaakov Benenson, Dr. Rivka Adar, Dr. Tamar Paz-Elizur, Prof. Zvi Livneh and Prof. Ehud Shapiro, of the Departments of Biological Chemistry and of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute.
According to Guinness, all of them are from Israel.
The device was awarded the Guinness World Record as the "smallest biological computing device".
According to the Guinness World Records website, the record for the smallest biological computing device was set on 20 February 2003.
Shapiro said that the researchers added an input module and an output module to the earlier molecular computer.
The computer is so small that a trillion of them fit in a drop of water.
The input mechanism is designed to assess concentrations of specific RNA molecules. Depending on the type of cancer, the body may overproduce or underproduce them.
The computer makes its diagnosis based on the detected RNA levels, using medical knowledge programmed into it in advance.
It exploits the base-pairing properties of DNA to detect mRNAs that indicate disease.
The computer is a long DNA hairpin. In its bend is the drug molecule, a short strand of DNA that interferes with gene regulation.
The computer checks four genes whose activity is abnormal in prostate cancer, in order to establish whether the typical markers of the disease are present.
Only if all four genes are abnormally active is the drug released.

In response to a cancer diagnosis, the output unit can initiate the controlled release of a single-stranded DNA molecule. This molecule is known to interfere with the cancer cell's activity and cause it to self-destruct.

stations.title: In the test tube: prostate and lung

paragraphs.text: In a series of test-tube experiments, the team programmed the computer to identify RNA molecules that indicate prostate cancer. After a correct diagnosis, the computer released short DNA strands designed to kill cancer cells.
The researchers successfully applied the computer to a test system that recreates, in a test tube, the typical molecular signatures of prostate cancer.
The team also identified, in a test tube, signs of one form of lung cancer.
According to Chemistry World, Shapiro's group claims to have created a DNA automaton that can "diagnose" and "treat" cancer symptoms, at least in a test tube.
On 28 April 2004 Shapiro and his colleagues reported in Nature the creation of the first molecular computer that could have medical use.
Shapiro also presented the findings at a symposium in Brussels.
Shapiro said that this is the first proof that the idea is workable. According to him, it is also the first demonstration of a possible real-life application of such a computer.
He said that only two years earlier they had predicted that it would take another 10 years to reach this point.
According to Chemistry World, the work brings the non-natural applications of DNA back to the real world, after they had until then been a molecular playground.
According to a quote from AFP, the vision of a molecular medical team that would be injected into a patient, identify a disease and treat it has come a step closer to reality.

In 2012, on the occasion of the Turing centenary year, the British Royal Academy asked Shapiro to take part in a special scientific publication, and he gave it an article he had written 14 years earlier, adding a description of the developments in the field since then.

stations.title: The vision: a doctor inside the cell

paragraphs.text: Shapiro said that one day the medical computer might be administered as a drug. It would be distributed throughout the body by the bloodstream and detect disease markers in every cell on its own.
Instead of biopsies that are analyzed in the laboratory, the DNA computer could diagnose the disease within the tissue in the body.
According to the report, the computer could enable doctors to treat cancer in its early stages, before tumours form. It could also deliver drugs to cells that are hard to reach.
In a 2011 lecture, Shapiro described chemotherapy as a non-selective treatment that kills all the cells that divide quickly.
In a 2012 article in Makor Rishon, Shapiro said that a "dumb drug", like the drugs of today, acts in the body everywhere and at all times, even when it is not needed.
According to him, programmable drugs will be able to be more powerful, because they will have fewer side effects.

According to a 2012 article in Makor Rishon, under laboratory conditions the nanocomputers work well. They enter a living cell, identify from the outside a situation that requires a response, and release a drug.

In 2021 Benenson and his colleagues at ETH Zurich reported on a different biological computer: a programmable genetic circuit delivered into cells inside an engineered virus. In an experiment on mice with liver cancer, the tumours disappeared in the mice that received the full computer.
The team was headed by Prof. Ehud Shapiro.
The team also included research students Yaakov Benenson, Binyamin Gil and Uri Ben-Dor, and Dr. Rivka Adar.
They worked at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot.
The research was supported by, among others, the Moross Institute for Cancer Research and the Samuel R. Dweck Foundation.
Shapiro's research in 2003 was supported, among others, by the Dolfi and Lola Ebner Center, Yad Hanadiv and the Robert Rees Fund.

stations.title: The obstacles on the way to the human body

paragraphs.text: The experiments were carried out in a test tube.
Shapiro acknowledged that there are very many obstacles, and that the road could take decades.
One question is how long the computer would survive in the body.
According to Chemistry World, the very introduction of the genetic material into a person who may be healthy would also need to be considered carefully.
Unlike the test tube, the body may contain edited mRNAs or protein factors that bind to the DNA computer in ways that are hard to predict.

disagreements.question: How long will it take until such a system works in the body?

versions.says: Shapiro in 2004: it may take decades
Makor Rishon in 2012: according to a cautious estimate, within 5 to 10 years there will be a first biological nanorobot for use
